column2: Q4 "cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, goats" in Fertile Crescent
column5: Horses were domesticated on the Eurasian steppe (Botai/Pontic-Caspian), not in the Fertile Crescent; standard Fertile Crescent domesticates are cattle, pigs, sheep, goats
column6: Removed "horses" from the Fertile Crescent list

column2: Q0 "the Andes (potatoes, ca. 3500 BCE)"
column5: Potato domestication near Lake Titicaca is dated about 7,000-10,000 years ago (FAO about 8,000 years ago); 3500 BCE is only the earliest direct consumption evidence (PNAS 2016, doi 10.1073/pnas.1604265113)
column6: Changed date to "ca. 8000-5000 BCE"

column2: Core Idea "About 10,000 years ago" vs Explainer "About 12,000 years ago"
column5: Internal inconsistency; Explainer's own dating (Fertile Crescent cultivation by about 9000 BCE) puts the start about 11,000-12,000 years ago
column6: Core Idea now "Beginning about 12,000 years ago"

column2: monsoon winds: northeast in summer, southwest in winter
column5: By convention the Indian Ocean summer monsoon is the southwest monsoon and the winter monsoon the northeast monsoon (winds named for where they blow from)
column6: Swapped to "southwest in summer, northeast in winter"

column2: Core Idea "(roughly 1500-1800)"
column5: Trade continued to Brazil until about 1850 and Cuba into the 1860s; file's own Explainer says 1500-1875 (Slave Voyages database coverage)
column6: Changed to "(roughly 1500-1870)"

column2: Core Idea "it was an aberration — that free labor is more productive"
column5: Contested claim stated as fact; Fogel and Engerman, Time on the Cross (1974), argued slave plantations were efficient
column6: Reframed as a debate: many economists hold free labor more productive, Fogel and Engerman argued plantations were efficient

column2: Core Idea "gold standard, fixed exchange rates, and independent monetary policy"
column5: Impossible trinity (Mundell-Fleming) is fixed exchange rates, free capital mobility, independent monetary policy, as the file's last question states
column6: Replaced "a gold standard" with "free capital movement" in the trilemma

column2: Shultz "the most important economic decision since FDR"
column5: Searches (Nixon Foundation, State Dept history, Garten's Three Days at Camp David reviews) found no source for this quote or attribution; per instructions removed unverifiable detail
column6: Removed the quote and attribution; sentence ends at "closing the gold window."

column2: Consumer society ... did not exist before the 20th century
column5: McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb, The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982), and de Vries's industrious revolution place a consumer revolution in 18th-century Britain and the Netherlands
column6: Now "reached its mass form only in the 20th century, though historians trace an earlier consumer revolution in 18th-century Britain and the Netherlands"

column2: Explainer "its production rested entirely on enslaved labor"
column5: Free peasant producers grew cotton in India and later Egypt (Beckert, Empire of Cotton); US slave-grown cotton dominated but was not all
column6: entirely to "largely"; same overstatement in Core Idea ("almost entirely") also changed to "largely"

column2: Core Idea "slavery's centrality to early modern capitalism"
column5: The file discusses the 19th century; "early modern" conventionally means about 1500-1800
column6: Changed to "19th-century capitalism"

column2: Explainer "roughly stable at 1-2 billion for centuries"
column5: UN/Our World in Data: world population first reached 1 billion about 1800 and 2 billion about 1927; it was below 1 billion in all earlier centuries
column6: Now "had grown slowly for millennia before passing 1 billion around 1800 and 2 billion around 1927"

column2: Q2 explanation "(for Africa) was used as forced labor through slavery"
column5: Garbled: the Atlantic slave trade was not an outlet for demographic-transition population growth, and the 19th-century European surplus went to settler colonies
column6: Now "much of it went to the Americas, Australia, and other settler colonies"

column2: Q1 option "funded by DARPA to enable resilient communications"
column5: Internet Society, Brief History of the Internet (internetsociety.org/internet/history-internet/brief-history-internet/): ARPANET was built for resource sharing, the nuclear-survivability idea came from Paul Baran's RAND work; agency was ARPA until 1972
column6: Option now "funded by the Pentagon's ARPA (later DARPA) to let research computers share resources"; explanation now credits resilience idea to Baran's RAND work and states ARPANET's resource-sharing purpose

column2: Q4 and Explainer "Robert Allen found that enclosed farms did achieve higher agricultural productivity"
column5: Allen, Enclosure and the Yeoman (1992) and EJ 1982: open-field yeomen made much of the productivity gain; enclosure mainly raised rents. Higher-yield finding is Heldring, Robinson and Vollmer (NBER w29772)
column6: Q4 answer attributes higher yields to the parish study and states Allen's contrary view; Explainer now says Allen argued open-field farmers had made many gains and enclosure mainly shifted income to landlords

column2: Q0 explanation "James Watt's steam engine (1769) helped solve" mine flooding
column5: Newcomen's atmospheric engine (1712) was the first used to pump mines; Watt's 1769 patent improved efficiency (Britannica, Newcomen engine); the file's Explainer says the same
column6: Now "steam engines ... first Thomas Newcomen's (1712) and later James Watt's more efficient design (patented 1769)"

column2: Q1 true-false Mesopotamian salinization "a major factor in the decline"
column5: Jacobsen and Adams, Science 1958, proposed it; Powell, Zeitschrift fur Assyriologie 75 (1985), "a critique of the theory of progressive salinization", disputed the yield data; stated as settled fact
column6: Statement now "Historians have argued that salinization ... contributed to the decline" (answer true stays correct); explanation attributes the thesis to Jacobsen and Adams and notes Powell's critique

column2: Explainer "10 Hours Act (1847) limited textile workers to 10-hour days"
column5: Factories Act 1847 limited women and young persons (13-18) in textile mills; adult men not directly covered (UK Parliament living heritage pages)
column6: Now "limited women and young persons in textile mills to 10-hour days (adult men were not directly covered)"

column2: Explainer Soviet 1932-33 and Chinese 1959-61 "were the largest famines in human history"
column5: Chinese 1959-61 is the deadliest recorded; Soviet 1932-33 (about 5.5-8.7 million USSR-wide) is not clearly larger than the 1876-79 North China famine (9-13 million)
column6: Now "The Chinese famine was the deadliest in recorded history, and both were made by state policy"

column2: Explainer Bengal 1943 food "available and being exported"
column5: Sen, Poverty and Famines (1981), rests on entitlement and purchasing-power failure, not exports; exports are not part of his Bengal argument
column6: Removed "and being exported"

column2: Q3 explanation "or offshore domestically (moving production to another country but keeping it in-house)"
column5: Self-contradiction inside the file's own definitions (offshoring is moving abroad)
column6: Now "or offshore in-house (moving production to another country but keeping it within the firm)"

column2: Explainer "depended on unique conditions — British hegemony, limited capital mobility"
column5: 1870-1914 had high capital mobility (Obstfeld and Taylor); the same Explainer says "Capital flowed freely across borders"
column6: Removed "limited capital mobility" from the list

column2: Q1 explanation Smoot-Hawley "helped turn an American recession into a global depression"
column5: Irwin, Peddling Protectionism (2011), and Eichengreen judge its output effect modest relative to monetary causes; stated too strongly
column6: Now says it deepened trade fragmentation and soured relations, most economic historians judge its output effect modest vs monetary causes; "widely considered one of the most consequential" softened to "often cited as a major policy mistake"

column2: Explainer "Civilian Conservation Corps employed 300,000 young men"
column5: About 3 million men served in the CCC 1933-1942 (Britannica, Civilian Conservation Corps); 300,000 was roughly the 1933 initial enrollment
column6: Now "enrolled about 3 million young men ... over its life (1933-1942)"

column2: Q1 "Dried and salted cod (stockfish)"
column5: Stockfish (torrfisk) is unsalted air-dried cod; salted dried cod is klippfisk (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockfish)
column6: Option now "Air-dried cod (stockfish)"; explanation "when air-dried (without salt)"

column2: Q4 "The Hamburg and Lubeck Borse (early commodity markets) developed price information systems"
column5: Hamburg exchange founded 1558 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Stock_Exchange; HBS Baker Library), after the League's peak (file dates it 1250-1550)
column6: Removed that sentence

column2: Q4 "marine insurance contracts appeared in Hanseatic ports in the 14th-15th centuries"
column5: Marine insurance originated in Italy, but one legal history source (vLex, Marine Insurance chapter) says Hanseatic merchants practised it contemporaneously; could not confirm the slow-adoption claim
column6: none

column2: Explainer "Their invention of the letter of credit ... double-entry bookkeeping (attributed to Luca Pacioli, 1494)"
column5: Bills of exchange and letters of credit were used by Italian merchants from the 13th century, before the Medici bank (1397); Pacioli's Summa (1494) was the first printed description of double-entry, not its origin (Britannica, Luca Pacioli)
column6: Now "Their skilled use of the letter of credit and bill of exchange (instruments Italian merchants had used since the 13th century) ... double-entry bookkeeping (already in use, and first described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494)"

column2: Core Idea banking "emerged in medieval Europe" vs Explainer ancient Mesopotamia
column5: Internal inconsistency; Explainer places earliest banking in Mesopotamian temples and says modern banking emerged in medieval Italy
column6: Now "has ancient roots, but its modern form emerged in medieval Europe"

column2: Q3 "Title IX of the Higher Education Act (1972)" and option D
column5: Title IX is part of the Education Amendments of 1972 (US Dept of Education, ed.gov Title IX overview)
column6: Explanation now "Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972"; option D now "passing Title IX"

column2: Q3 true-false phrased as "What strategic goal motivated it?"
column5: Malformed item: open question typed true-false
column6: Rewritten as statement "Bismarck introduced ... insurance ... mainly out of humanitarian concern for workers' welfare." answer false (unchanged); removed "trick question" opener

column5: SPD became the largest Reichstag party in 1912; German Revolution of 1918-19 ended the empire
column6: Now says the bet had mixed results: SPD kept growing (largest party 1912), empire fell in 1918-19, social insurance model endured

column2: Explainer "major shipping losses ... the 1906 San Francisco earthquake"
column5: 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire was a land (non-marine) loss, famously paid by Lloyd's non-marine underwriters (Cuthbert Heath)
column6: major shipping losses to "major losses"; added "(a non-marine loss)"

column2: Core Idea money "emerges when communities need a medium of exchange beyond barter"
column5: Contradicts the file's own Q0 and Explainer (Graeber; Sumerian credit records), which reject barter origins
column6: Now "emerges when communities need shared ways to measure debts and settle exchanges"

column2: Q3 true-false phrased as "What problem did the absence of central banking create?"
column5: Malformed item: open question typed true-false
column6: Rewritten as statement "Because the United States had no central bank from 1836 to 1913, its money supply was inelastic: it could not readily expand during financial panics." answer true (unchanged, matches explanation)

column2: Q1 explanation "The Song Dynasty initially issued notes ... (feiqian, 'flying money')"
column5: Feiqian (flying money) was a Tang-dynasty (9th-century) draft; Song-era jiaozi began as private Sichuan notes (Britannica, paper money / feiqian)
column6: Now attributes flying money to the Tang and jiaozi receipts to private Sichuan shops under the Song

column2: Explainer "Bitcoin lost 80% of its value in 2022"
column5: BTC about $46,300 on 1 Jan 2022 and about $16,500 on 31 Dec 2022, a fall of about 64%
column6: Now "lost about two-thirds of its value in 2022"

column2: Core Idea "regressive taxes (same rate for all)"
column5: A single rate on income is proportional (flat); a regressive tax takes a smaller share as income rises, as the file's own misconception bullet on sales tax says
column6: Now "regressive taxes (taking a smaller share of income as income rises, as sales taxes often do)"

column2: Q3 true-false phrased as "What is the difference between tax avoidance and tax evasion...?"
column5: Malformed item: open question typed true-false; answer false conflicted with explanation saying there is a difference
column6: Rewritten as "Tax avoidance and tax evasion are legally the same thing, since both reduce the tax a person pays." answer false; explanation opener now "There is a meaningful legal difference"

column5: Malformed item: open question typed true-false; Factory Act 1833 created four paid inspectors (UK Parliament living heritage)
column6: Rewritten as "...first effective factory legislation because, unlike earlier acts, it created paid government inspectors with power to enforce it." answer true (unchanged)

column2: Explainer Rome Gini 0.43-0.50 "comparable to ... Brazil or South Africa"
column5: World Bank Gini: Brazil about 52 (2022), South Africa about 63 (2014); Rome estimates (Scheidel and Friesen) are lower
column6: Now "high by modern standards, though below the most unequal modern societies such as Brazil (about 0.52) or South Africa (about 0.63)"

column2: Core Idea "Global inequality has not clearly trended ... (increasing global inequality)"
column5: Milanovic, Global Inequality (2016), and World Inequality Report: global interpersonal inequality rose from 1820 into the late 20th century and has fallen since about 2000, driven by China and India
column6: Now states the rise then fall since about 2000, mainly from China and India growth, while many poor countries remained poor

column2: Q3 true-false phrased as "Why is domestic work structurally prone to informality?"
column5: Malformed item: open question typed true-false
column6: Rewritten as "Paid domestic work ... has historically been among the most informal categories of labor, partly because it takes place in private homes that are hard to inspect." answer true (unchanged, matches explanation point 1)

column2: Q4 "UK and California courts ... both ruled Uber drivers are employees"
column5: Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5 held drivers are "workers", an intermediate status; California Superior Court (Aug 2020, affirmed Oct 2020) found drivers likely employees under AB5
column6: Now states UK Supreme Court 2021 "workers" ruling and California 2020 "likely employees" finding

column5: Seven police officers and at least four civilians died (Chicago Historical Society; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haymarket_affair)
column6: Now "In all, seven police officers and at least four civilians died"

column5: Knights' national leader Terence Powderly opposed the May 1886 strike (secret circular); the strike was called by the Federation of Organized Trades and Labor Unions, with many local Knights assemblies joining

column5: Britannica (Homestead Strike) and Pennsylvania historical marker: at least seven workers and three Pinkertons killed
column6: Now "at least seven workers and three Pinkertons"

column2: Explainer "By 1400 in England, serfdom had largely disappeared"
column5: Mark Bailey, The Decline of Serfdom in Late Medieval England (2014): villein tenure shed main dues c.1370-1410, personal servility dwindled to irrelevance by the mid-15th century, last vestiges in the 16th
column6: Now "By the mid-15th century ... serfdom had largely disappeared; most peasants were tenants paying money rents"

column5: In English legal usage villein and serf both denote unfree peasants (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villein); lower holders were cottars and bordars

column5: Same misattribution as enclosure-movement: Allen, Enclosure and the Yeoman (1992), argued open-field farmers made many gains and enclosure mainly raised rents; Heldring, Robinson and Vollmer (NBER w29772) find higher yields

column5: English East India Company (1600) and Muscovy Company (1553) were earlier joint-stock companies; VOC is usually called the first permanent joint-stock company with publicly traded shares
column6: Now "the first permanent joint-stock company with publicly traded shares"

column2: Explainer Potosi "perhaps 40,000 tons" vs Q0 40,000 tons entering Europe 1500-1800
column5: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_silver_trade_from_the_16th_to_19th_centuries: Spanish American mines produced about 40,000 tons in the two centuries after 1545 (all mines, not Potosi alone, and not a Europe-arrival figure)
column6: Explainer and Q0 now both say Spanish America (Potosi plus Mexican mines) produced perhaps 40,000 tons in the two centuries after 1545; Q0 adds "much of it shipped to Europe"

column5: Unequal treaties (1858, 1866 tariff convention) capped Japan's tariffs at about 5% until tariff autonomy in 1911
